title: Light of Day
dateline: Selrick Academy, the hall. The day the newcomers became Aspirants.
mood: A fish market under a torn dome, a great lady who will not land early, and someone quietly counting the seconds.

hero.alt: Official art: pink-haired Guinevere hangs high above the city with her fists raised, two round cat-eared drones with yellow ring eyes beside her and spiny Enders at the edges of the sky.

segs.t: Layla stood under the five great stars in her combat suit, with Fanny, Ruby and Angela in a row beside her. Lesley was on the last words of her speech about trust.
When it ended, Layla turned around. Along the wall, a pink-haired girl was waving her whole arm at a black-haired girl by the door.
She’s talked to me exactly once,
thought Layla.
The fish market.
The gate portal. Weeks earlier.
The raid that mattered was on a shore ward. At the portal, a pink-haired girl stopped in front of Layla with her chin up.
“You’re Layla. I’m the great lady Guinevere. Nobody’s introduced us.”
“You’re on a billboard.”
“Yes,” said Guinevere, delighted. “That’s me.”
“Vexana,” said the black-haired girl beside her, in case it was needed. Her eyes were violet, and a small mole sat beside her mouth.
She and Layla had shared classes for two years. Neither had ever spoken first.
Two years of nothing,
thought Layla.
Now I have a team, and she talks. She went first. One to her.
Professor Joe saw the third years off at the gate portal every day now, still on his cane. Most days it meant a handful of Enders.
“Fish market,” he said. “The dome’s torn over the stalls. Layla-Fanny Team, the west end. You two, the east.”
Guinevere walked into the portal’s light as if it had been lit for her. Vexana went after her without a word.

The portal let Layla out on wet cobbles that smelled of fish and salt. The stall keepers had run at the siren and left their aprons on the hooks. At the west end, Fanny drew her blades. “Let’s do our best together.”
“Behind me,” said Layla, and went first.
The east end, the same minute.

Guinevere hung in the mouth of the tear on wings of light. The tear was a black gash in the dome, right above the stalls. Enders dropped through it, tall and gray. Crates burst under their feet. Fish slid across the stones.
Her two drones circled her, round and gray, with cat ears and yellow ring eyes. Drones and wings both ran on her aspirant power.
She met the Enders with her fists as they came through. A big one squeezed through the gash and swung at her. For the blow, its chest plates opened on a glowing core. Guinevere pulled back her fist.
“Light of day, pour down.”
Light poured from her drones into the open chest, and her fist went in after it. The Ender fell toward the roofs. Vexana’s bolt met it on the way down.
Vexana kept to the roof below, where she could see the tear and the street at once. Whatever Guinevere knocked down, her staff finished. Guinevere never looked back to check.
Vexana is there.
Once, a claw came over the lip of the tear and caught at her boot. She did not turn. A bolt went up past her heel, and the claw let go.

Around the thirtieth minute, her arms went heavy. Her drones flew a hand lower on each pass, and their yellow rings dimmed a shade. She hung lower too. The tear was above her now, and the roofs were close.
A great lady does not land early.
She punched harder.
Her wings went out like a switch.
She dropped, and her drones dropped with her. The wind tore at her ponytail. A gutter flashed past, then the edge of a roof.
A hand closed on her wrist and stopped her with a jerk.
Vexana is there.
This time Guinevere looked. Vexana lay flat on the tiles with one arm over the edge. She hauled Guinevere up and rolled her onto the roof.
Guinevere got to her knees.
“Ngh... this is a lady’s refinement. It’s the way to regain your elegance in three seconds.”
Vexana counted under her breath. Guinevere got to her feet, straightened her bow and lifted her chin. One drone rose off the tiles, its ring lit. The other did not come.
“Four,” said Vexana.
Vexana’s hand was shaking. She closed it around her staff until it stopped.
I saw it a minute ago,
she thought.
I said nothing.
On another raid she had called up to Guinevere to come down and rest. Guinevere had flown higher. If Vexana had flown up beside her, Guinevere would have known she had been seen.
So she had gone to the edge of the roof and waited.

For the rest of the raid, Guinevere fought on the tiles with her fists, her one drone at her shoulder. Vexana stood on the ridge behind her, a step nearer than before, and fired over her shoulder. Neither of them mentioned it.
When the last Ender lay among the fish, a medic took Guinevere’s wrist to tape it. Vexana found the other drone in the gutter. One ear was bent flat, and the bracket under it was twisted.
She picked it up without asking. While the medic was still taping, she went back through the portal with it, ahead of the others. She said nothing about that either.

That night Guinevere lay in bed in her room at the Academy, the lamp off and the door open a hand’s width, as always. Stuffed animals crowded the wall side of the bed. Her wrist was taped. On the shelf, the drone charger glowed, with one cradle empty.
Lost on a fish-market roof,
she thought.
Of all the places for a lady to lose a drone.
At the usual hour, the phone buzzed on her pillow.
“Go to bed,” said Vexana.
“I’m in bed.”
“Good.”
A pause. Guinevere looked up into the dark. “About the roof. It was a crosswind, that’s all. It...”
“Go to bed.”
Click.

Guinevere put the phone back on the pillow. She lay awake. Her wrist throbbed where Vexana’s hand had closed on it. Under her breath she counted, the way someone used to count for her whenever she fell.
“One. Two. Three.”
